doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Varying pay, career choices, and life on the road
summary: Sliding pay scales, the Spain trip decision, learning languages and road routines.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Right. It seems like every particular job always requires, in addition to the back and forth with the money, there’s always something a little bit different about every job. How much room do we have on stage? What are the acoustics like? It’s never like when a person goes to work every single day, knows what his office is like, and he knows who he’s going to be dealing with every day for the most part.

That’s right. And the monetary scales are so sliding. You can’t even believe it. When people ask, you know I’ll do a college workshop and they ask questions like well how much do you make and things like that, it’s really hard to tell somebody. Because you can play in New York and you make a hundred dollars at a club. You play a concert you make a few thousand. And somewhere at the end it all balances out to a pretty nice living. But it’s never constant, and you always have to make these decisions. Like you make monetary decisions and you make career decisions. For example the Spain trip, they don’t have that much money over there. I’m not making huge tons of money, but I don’t play Spain often enough that I should pass on it. So it’s been a few years since I’ve been there, I like being there and I feel like I need to go there. So I’ll do three weeks there, come home with a modest amount of money, and then I’ve got a bunch of really good paying things after that in November and December that’ll make up for it. So it’s always like that.
You know it’s funny, I actually learned enough to get by in the countries, and I bone up on it before I go, and then I forget it again afterwards. And I’m learning Swedish now of course.
You say “let’s take a break” in eleven different languages.

But, “what time does the next train leave?” No, but I try to learn a little bit of the language. And I like to be in these countries and check out the museums. I love to walk and I’ve worked out some kind of a discipline plan for my road tours. I listen to a lot of music, I read a lot too, I read all kinds of books, fiction, non-fiction, everything. I just am a very curious kind of person. So that gets me through the tours.
